 Trivia covering the 1621 Plymouth feast, Lincoln's 1863 holiday, FDR's date change, and the first Macy's parade balloons.
 1 / 17 List slides 15 Thanksgiving facts, from a 1621 harvest feast to the first parade balloons List slides Previous Start over By Cris Tolomia · Updated October 29, 2026 Add QZ to Google Illustration: Quartz
 Every November, Americans sit down to a holiday whose origin story feels familiar, yet the documentation behind it has gaps. Thanksgiving stands among the best-loved national celebrations in the country, and today it revolves around food, family, friends, and fun. The turkey, the pie, the parade, and the football game all carry an air of permanence, as though they had belonged to the occasion from the start. Each of those customs has a distinct backstory, with dates, names, and decisions attached. Knowing where they began turns a routine meal into a livelier conversation, and it hands every guest something worth repeating between courses.
 The November 1621 gathering of Plymouth Colony settlers and the Wampanoag, the scene most people picture, comes down to us in thin detail. Edward Winslow, an English settler, wrote the best surviving account in a letter, and he never called the event "Thanksgiving." He described a harvest festivity that stretched across several days, with a three-day banquet that drew King Massasoit and 90 Wampanoag men. Beyond that outline, specifics run short. Over the following centuries, a feast that earned a passing mention swelled into something sprawling. Each generation layered its own notion of gratitude on top, and the additions stacked up until legend and evidence grew hard to separate. Thanksgiving's early chapters read as a muddle, leaving room for half-remembered tales to pass as settled fact.
 History.com sorts through that tangle in a question-and-answer explainer by Dave Roos, who writes for the site and contributes to the podcast Stuff You Should Know. The piece debuted Nov. 12, 2018, and its latest update came Sept. 3, 2026. It poses 15 questions and answers each one, moving from the Pilgrims' plates through presidential traditions to the Macy's $M parade, over a span that runs from 1621 into the 20th century. The article assigns no scores, conducts no survey, and puts its entries in no ranked order, so each question works on its own. The publisher pitches it as trivia for the dinner table.
 Plymouth shares its first-feast claim with Florida 
 Illustration: Quartz
 In 1621, colonists in Plymouth, Massachusetts, and their Wampanoag neighbors sat down to an autumn harvest feast that many people regard as one of the first Thanksgiving celebrations. Even the standard description of the Plymouth meal stops at "one of the first" and withholds sole possession of the title. The hedge carries weight. The Plymouth gathering supplies the scene most people picture when they think of the holiday.
 Florida draws a rival claim from some historians, who contend the state, and not Massachusetts, may hold the distinction of first Thanksgiving site in North America. Their argument shifts the holiday's starting point away from New England and beyond the Pilgrim story.
 The two positions measure different things. Plymouth's standing rests on a harvest meal that English settlers shared with a Native American people. Florida's case turns on geography and asks where on the continent the observance first took place. A gathering can be the best remembered without being the earliest, and the Plymouth feast may fit that description.
 Hedged wording runs through both sides of the debate — "one of the first" for Plymouth, "may hold" for Florida — and leaves neither location with a clean title. Neither side has produced a verdict that closes the matter. The holiday's birthplace remains an open question at its most basic level, an uncertainty that sits awkwardly beside the familiar origin story retold each November.
 Plymouth's grip on the holiday comes from memory and imagery, and its title as the first site remains contested.
 This slide runs about 245 words, short of the 300-word minimum. The source offers only two facts on this subject: the 1621 Plymouth feast as one of the first celebrations and some historians' contention that Florida may hold the first-site title. It gives no details of the Florida claim, and no approved web details cover it. Further expansion would require padding or invented facts.
 The 1621 feast went without mashed potatoes 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The 1621 Plymouth feast went without mashed potatoes, and timing explains the absence. Potatoes had crossed from South America to Europe a short while earlier. The tuber remained a newcomer in the Old World when the colonists gathered with the Wampanoag. A bowl of mashed spuds had no path to their plates. Anyone who pictures that side dish at the first celebration has carried a later custom back into the 17th century.
 No surviving record places a large roasted turkey on the 1621 table, even though the bird is native to the region. The settlers and their guests had turkeys within reach, yet no account confirms that anyone cooked one. At this early meal, the centerpiece of the modern holiday rests on guesswork. Families who carve a bird each November are honoring a tradition the written evidence cannot trace to Plymouth.
 Deer arrived with the Wampanoag and gave the menu one of its few confirmed meats. The guests supplied part of the meal themselves, which casts the gathering as a shared undertaking between the two groups. Mussels, lobster, and bass, all of which the nearby coast could supply, stood among the probable seafood offerings. Produce from the first Pilgrim harvest, pumpkin among it, rounded out the likely spread. Pumpkin's presence suggests at least one of today's staples had a seat at the outset, though how cooks prepared it goes unrecorded.
 Squanto, also called Tisquantum, gave the Pilgrims a guide and a voice in their new surroundings. He interpreted for the Plymouth Colony newcomers and led them to food sources. His work as an interpreter gave the settlers and the Wampanoag a way to talk across a language divide. The colony might not have survived without his help. Venison the Wampanoag carried in and the guidance Squanto offered point to a celebration that leaned on Native knowledge of the land no less than on the Pilgrims' first crops.
 The first national Thanksgiving honored Saratoga 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The Continental Congress called for a countrywide day of Thanksgiving on Dec. 18, 1777, and tied the day to the American victory over the British at the Battle of Saratoga. The choice put a military triumph at the center of the first observance meant for the entire country. Gratitude, in this early form, answered the turns of a war.
 A December date also set the 1777 observance apart from the November gathering at Plymouth. Congress fixed its day of thanks to news from the front, with no harvest calendar in view. The national holiday began as a reply to one event, and its timing followed that event.
 Wartime thanks set the pattern for several decades afterward. Thanksgiving days arrived at irregular intervals, and presidents often announced them during or after major clashes. The holiday held no settled spot on the calendar and did not yet qualify as an established national occasion. Each new observance depended on events in the field and on a leader choosing to mark them. Nobody could say whether or when the next one would come.
 Washington issued another call in 1789, after the Revolutionary War closed in American success. His proclamation followed the logic of the Saratoga observance, with a military result supplying the reason for a public pause. The 1777 and 1789 calls bracketed the conflict, one celebrating a single victory and the other its conclusion. In its first national form, the holiday took its cue from the fighting, a long way from a harvest table.
 Thomas Jefferson refused to proclaim thanksgiving days 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Thomas Jefferson declined to issue any proclamation setting aside a day of thanksgiving, and he stands as the president who would not recognize the observance. His refusal set him apart from the leaders before and after him who did call for such days. The decision carried weight because the custom had no footing of its own. Nothing fixed a date on the calendar, and no yearly habit carried the celebration from one administration to the next.
 Jefferson's stance exposes how much the early holiday hinged on a single officeholder. A countrywide day of thanks existed only when a president chose to announce one. One person's refusal could leave the country without a shared celebration for as long as he held power.
 Abraham Lincoln fixed the final Thursday in 1863 
 Illustration: Quartz
 President Abraham Lincoln turned Thanksgiving into a yearly national observance in 1863. His decree counts as the first official Thanksgiving, and it handed the country an annual feast day it could plan around. Earlier days of thanks had hinged on a leader choosing to declare one, and they arrived in fits and starts.
 Gatherings of gratitude reach back to the earliest European settlements. Lincoln's contribution was repetition. A one-time order fades once its occasion passes. A recurring holiday builds habits, expectations, and family rituals that outlive any single administration. A countrywide date gave households a shared rhythm the scattered earlier occasions never offered. The first proclamation still stopped short of the whole map. In the middle of the Civil War, Confederate states did not consider themselves subject to Lincoln's order. Customs that arrived much later, such as the Macy's $M parade and its balloons, found a dependable date waiting for them once the habit took hold.
 Lincoln pinned the celebration to the final Thursday in November, setting the original precedent for its scheduling. Tying the feast to a weekday kept it off any fixed point on the calendar, so the exact date shifted from one year to the next. In a November with four Thursdays, his formula and today's fourth-Thursday date fall on the same day. In a November with five, Lincoln's rule lands a week later than the modern date.
 The final-Thursday standard held sway into the 20th century. Franklin D. Roosevelt's eventual push to restore the final Thursday, after his own early-date experiment, shows Lincoln's choice carried weight generations after he made it. A president who had broken the pattern ended up steering back toward it, the clearest measure of how deep Lincoln's timing ran.
 Sarah Josepha Hale pushed for Lincoln's proclamation 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Sarah Josepha Hale, a writer and abolitionist, may have made the difference between a national Thanksgiving and no proclamation at all in 1863. Her campaign succeeded, and it earned her the nickname "Mother of Thanksgiving."
 The nickname hands parentage of the holiday to an author. Lincoln made the announcement, yet the honor for its existence flows to the woman who argued for it, a measure of the weight her advocacy carried.
 Hale sold the observance as a civic remedy. She believed a unifying gesture could ease the tensions building across the country in the years before the Civil War. Her argument framed one shared day of gratitude as common ground for a public pulling apart. The case handed a harvest custom a political job, turning a meal into a tool for cohesion.
 The Library of Congress reports that Hale spent years writing to other government officials before she carried her appeal to Lincoln. Her letter to the president went out on Sept. 28, 1863. She wrote that with his help, "the permanency and unity of our Great American Festival of Thanksgiving would be forever secured." The profile credits her determination, at least in part, with setting the precedent for the national holiday. The unity she hoped for did not arrive at once. Confederate states did not consider themselves subject to Lincoln's proclamation, and the country marked the day divided.
 Hale's reach extended past the holiday. She receives credit for writing the nursery rhyme about Mary and her little lamb. She also edited Godey's Lady's Book, a popular magazine for women, and used its pages to champion education for women and their right to own property. Her output stretched from a children's rhyme to a bid to reshape the country's calendar, an audience running from children to a president. Alongside her opposition to slavery, she pressed for schooling, property rights, and a day of thanks.
 Franklin D. Roosevelt moved Thanksgiving a week earlier 
 Illustration: Quartz
 President Franklin D. Roosevelt decreed in 1939 that Thanksgiving would arrive one week ahead of schedule, on the fourth of that November's five Thursdays. His motive came from the cash register. Roosevelt feared that a late holiday would shrink the Christmas shopping season. Custom at the time assigned the feast to the month's final Thursday, and a November holding five of them pushed the meal into the closing days before December. Advancing the holiday a week handed merchants seven more days of gift buying.
 The shift picked up the nickname "Franksgiving" along with a wave of anger. Thanksgiving traditionalists and Roosevelt's political rivals condemned the decision, and one critic went as far as comparing the president to Hitler. Twenty-three of the 48 states rejected the new date. Their refusal left the country marking one holiday on two different Thursdays. Close to half the states treated a presidential calendar order as something they could ignore. The split exposed how little weight a White House decree carried over a holiday that no federal law yet pinned to a date.
 Roosevelt stuck with the earlier Thursday in 1940 and 1941, stretching the experiment across three straight Novembers. His next step aimed to restore the final Thursday of November starting in 1942, a retreat to the timing his 1939 order had discarded.
 Congress acted before Roosevelt's planned 1942 reversion took effect. Lawmakers set Thanksgiving on the fourth Thursday of November, and the holiday has remained there since. The congressional rule bridged the two camps. In a November with four Thursdays, the fourth and the last fall on the same day, so backers of the final Thursday lose nothing in those years. In a five-Thursday year, the holiday lands on the date Roosevelt picked in 1939. Roosevelt abandoned his own change, yet the measure Congress adopted secured his preferred timing in every November with five Thursdays.
 Pumpkin pie anchored New England tables by the 1700s 
 Credit: KATRIN BOLOVTSOVA / Pexels
 Pumpkin pie had become a regular dish at New England Thanksgiving meals by the turn of the 18th century. Colonial cooks had plenty of alternatives. Early settlers baked pies filled with apples, pears, quince, and blueberries alongside pumpkin. Out of that wide choice, pumpkin emerged as the one New Englanders expected to see at the Thanksgiving feast.
 Colchester, Connecticut, delayed its 1705 Thanksgiving by a week, according to legend, after the town ran short of molasses. Without the sweetener, cooks could not bake their pies, and the community chose to wait. The story treats pumpkin pie as inseparable from the holiday itself. A town willing to push back a day of thanks over a missing dessert staple placed the pie closer to ritual than to garnish.
 Smithsonian Magazine reports that the first recorded recipe for pumpkin pie appeared in American Cookery, a book by the New England author Amelia Simmons. The Library of Congress describes American Cookery as the first cookbook by an American to reach print in America and notes that it offered two recipes for "pompkin" pudding in a pastry crust. Simmons made a filling closer to custard than to sliced pumpkin.
 Simmons stewed and strained her pumpkin before blending it with eggs, sugar, and cream or milk. She added molasses in some versions and spiced the mix with ginger, mace, nutmeg, and allspice. The molasses ties her formula to the ingredient the Colchester tale says the town lacked.
 Pumpkin pie kept its New England identity as its appeal widened. Most of its sales stayed in New England, where sellers promoted it as a regional specialty. Northern states earned a reputation for pumpkin pies as the country expanded west and distinct local pie traditions took shape. Across every account, from the Colchester lore to the cookbook era, the dessert stays bound to New England, whose holiday tables first made it a fixture.
 Cranberries doubled as a Native American dye 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Native Americans put cranberries to two distinct uses, eating the berries and turning them into a strong red dye. One crop served as both food and a source of color. The berry's worth to those communities extended beyond any table.
 Sweetened cranberry relish, a staple of many modern holiday menus, had little chance of reaching the 1621 harvest celebration. The Pilgrims had run through their sugar before November arrived. A sauce built on sweetness required the one pantry item the settlers could no longer supply. The condiment on today's holiday tables belongs to a later chapter than the berry itself.
 SHORTFALL NOTE: Slide 9 runs about 100 words against a 300-word minimum. The source gives only two facts for cranberries: Native Americans ate them and used them as a strong red dye, and the Pilgrims had used up their sugar before November 1621, so sweetened relish almost certainly did not appear at the first feast. The source's own heading asks when canning began, but the body gives no canning date or detail, and no approved web details cover cranberries. The slide stops where the evidence stops.
 Swanson TV dinners sold 10 million trays in 1954 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Swanson moved 10 million turkey TV dinners in 1954, its first full year of production. The product grew out of a surplus of Thanksgiving turkey. Extra holiday birds needed somewhere to go, and a ready-made meal offered an outlet. Selling that many units in a single full year shows demand arrived at once, with no long ramp-up.
 A Swanson salesman found the fix. He ordered 5,000 aluminum trays, built a turkey meal to fill them, and enlisted an assembly line of workers to put each dinner together. The result became the first TV tray dinner and a culinary hit. Each step solved a separate piece of the problem. The trays held the food, the meal design gave the dinner its form, and the workers supplied speed. The assembly line mattered as much as the recipe. Factory-style production let the company turn a seasonal glut into a product it could repeat at volume.
 The original menu set a serving of turkey beside cornbread stuffing, peas, and sweet potatoes. Turkey acted as the main course, with the stuffing and vegetables as its companions.
 Gerry Thomas said the packaged meals airlines gave passengers inspired the concept. His version traces the idea to travel catering, a long way from the holiday table. Thomas's telling has met resistance. The heirs of Clarke Swanson have disputed Thomas's claim to have invented the dish, and Swanson's own account of who devised the tray meal has shifted over time. The question of authorship remains open as a result. The dispute centers on credit for the idea.
 The 1954 total equaled 2,000 times the salesman's opening order of trays. An initial purchase counted in the thousands gave way to sales counted in the millions once production hit its stride. A holiday leftover had found a market that outlasted the November season.
 The presidential turkey pardon began with Bush in 1989 
 Illustration: Quartz
 George H.W. Bush turned the "pardoning" of a Thanksgiving turkey into a yearly White House tradition in 1989. His decision gave a permanent spot on the holiday calendar to a custom with roots in a harsher arrangement from decades earlier.
 Turkey farmers began sending presidents plump birds for the holidays in the 1940s. No reprieve came with those deliveries. The first family ate the turkeys as part of the season, and each gift from the growers ended on a dinner plate. Nothing in the routine set one bird apart from any other turkey bound for a platter.
 John F. Kennedy spared one of the donated birds in 1963. "We'll just let this one grow," he said. He added, "It's our Thanksgiving present to him." The second remark flipped the direction of the exchange. Farmers had handed the turkey to the president as an offering, and Kennedy returned a kindness of his own to the bird.
 Bush's 1989 move drew a line between two eras of the practice. Before that turning point, a turkey's survival hinged on the whim of whichever president accepted the bird, and Kennedy's quip supplies the example the record singles out. After 1989, clemency for a turkey became a scheduled annual event at the White House. The choice moved from one occupant's impulse to the office itself, which repeats it each November.
 The quotation marks around "pardoning" signal the joke inside the ceremony. The word casts a farm-raised bird as a recipient of presidential mercy and extends the playful tone Kennedy struck in 1963. A pardon implies a sentence to escape, and for these turkeys the sentence was the feast awaiting every bird farmers sent in the 1940s. Between those first deliveries and 1989, the bird's role inverted. The modern guest of honor walks away from the carving board its predecessors met.
 Football joined Thanksgiving before the NFL existed 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Football claimed a seat at the Thanksgiving table before anything called the NFL existed. Credit for the holiday matchup belongs to earlier players, and the league arrived to find the tradition in place.
 College rivalries spread the habit. Newspapers gave mounting attention to the yearly Princeton-Yale contest, and teams at other colleges and high schools around the country began holding grudge matches of their own on Thanksgiving Day. Student athletes on campuses and school fields made holiday football a nationwide fixture.
 The Coolidge family adopted a raccoon meant for dinner 
 Illustration: Quartz
 President Calvin Coolidge received a live raccoon as a Thanksgiving gift in 1926, and the sender meant it to end up on the holiday table. The Mississippi man who shipped the animal praised raccoon meat as "toothsome," a word that left no doubt about the meal he pictured.
 The shipment treated raccoon as fare worthy of a presidential feast. Sending the creature alive left the butchering and the cooking to the recipients.
 The Coolidges overruled the sender's plan. They adopted the raccoon, named her Rebecca, and kept her as a pet. She joined a household menagerie of exotic animals, a collection that marked the Coolidge home as anything but ordinary.
 Naming Rebecca moved her from the menu into the family circle. No ceremony, proclamation, or custom compelled the decision. The Coolidges made the call on their own, without public fanfare.
 Rebecca's rescue came as a private choice, before sparing a holiday animal grew into an official White House ritual. The episode shows a president could let a Thanksgiving animal shipped for eating live on, with no rule or rite to justify it.
 This slide runs about 180 words, short of the 300-word minimum. The source gives only the 1926 date, the Mississippi sender, the "toothsome" quote, the name Rebecca, and her place in the family's menagerie of exotic animals, and no approved web details cover the Coolidge raccoon. Further expansion would require padding or unsourced detail.
 The Macy's parade promised an animal circus 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Macy's $M drew its first Thanksgiving crowds with a three-part pledge of "magnificent floats," bands, and an "animal circus." The department store framed the procession as a spectacle, and its wording echoed the vocabulary of a traveling show. Macy's also put its own name on the event, a branding choice the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade still carries.
 The animal circus set the offer apart from its other two attractions. Floats and musicians suit any street march. A circus placed living creatures at the heart of the store's appeal and gave spectators a reason to turn out that an ordinary procession could not match.
 Each piece of the pledge reached the crowd in a different way. Floats gave onlookers something to watch, bands filled the street with sound, and animals brought motion and the novelty of live creatures along the route.
 By pairing those draws with its own name, a retailer turned a family holiday into an occasion for public entertainment, and the company's brand rode along from the first outing.
 Parade balloons replaced live zoo animals in 1927 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Macy's $M unveiled its first oversized balloons in 1927, and the debut lineup paired Felix the Cat with inflated elephants, tigers, and a giant hummingbird. Every shape in that roster depicted a creature, the cartoon cat included. The procession held on to its wildlife theme in a form that could not panic.
 Live zoo animals had carried that theme through the streets before the giants arrived. Marching in front of thousands of noisy revelers left them agitated. Crowds and clamor sat at the heart of the event. The beasts faced the very conditions that unsettled them each time the march stepped off.
 Inflatable stand-ins removed the strain and still put elephants and tigers before spectators. A tiger with nothing alive inside could face the din of a packed avenue without flinching, a test the living performers had failed. Organizers kept the menagerie imagery and shed the hazard of a rattled herd.
 Felix the Cat and the giant hummingbird reveal a second gain. No keeper can lead a cartoon character or an outsize bird down a city street, yet an inflated version of either could join the procession. Inflation freed the lineup from the limits of what a zoo could supply.
 Oxygen filled the 1927 debut pieces. Helium had no part in that original batch.
 Shortfall note: this slide runs about 215 words, under the 300-word minimum. The source gives only the 1927 debut, the four named balloon subjects, the agitation of live zoo animals before noisy crowds, and the oxygen fill, and no approved web details cover the parade balloons. No further genuine facts were available, so the slide stops where the substance runs out.
